title: Der Fuchs und die Frau Gevatterin
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 74. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, that, liebwerthe, müßt).
about: KHM 74, one of the wolf-and-fox fables the Grimms set among the household tales. The fox accepts the honour of standing godfather to the she-wolf’s cub, and repays it by sending her alone into a sheepfold, then lying at the entrance of the wood pretending to have been beaten to pieces so that she will carry him home on her back. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as liebwerthe, that (for tat), gieng and müßt.

sentences.t: Die Wölfin brachte ein Junges zur Welt und ließ den Fuchs zu Gevatter einladen.
sentences.l: The she-wolf brought a young one into the world and had the fox invited to be godfather.
sentences.i: The she-wolf brought a cub into the world, and had the fox invited to stand as godfather.
sentences.n: Gevatter is the old word for a godfather, and Gevatterin the courteous address the parties to a christening use for each other: the she-wolf is the mother, not a godmother, but the fox stands sponsor to her cub and so calls her Frau Gevatterin. English once had a word for exactly this — gossip, from god-sib — and has lost it. “zu Gevatter bitten” is the fixed phrase for asking someone to stand at a christening.

sentences.t: „Er ist doch nahe mit uns verwandt,“ sprach sie, „hat einen guten Verstand und viel Geschicklichkeit, er kann mein Söhnlein unterrichten und ihm in der Welt forthelfen.“
sentences.l: “He is after all closely related to us,” said she, “has a good understanding and much skill, he can instruct my little-son and help him forward in the world.”
sentences.i: “He is closely related to us, after all,” said she; “he has good sense and a deal of skill, and he can teach my little son and help him get on in the world.”
sentences.n: doch appeals to something both parties already know — “after all”. The second clause drops its subject: “hat einen guten Verstand” has no er, which German allows once the subject carries over.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs erschien auch ganz ehrbar und sprach „liebwerthe Frau Gevatterin, ich danke euch für die Ehre, die ihr mir erzeigt, ich will mich aber auch so halten, daß ihr eure Freude daran haben sollt.“
sentences.l: The fox appeared too quite respectable and said “dear-worthy Mistress Godmother, I thank you for the honour that you show me; but I will also conduct myself so that you shall have your joy in it.”
sentences.i: The fox appeared, respectable enough, and said: “Most esteemed Mistress Godmother, I thank you for the honour you do me, and I shall so conduct myself that you will have joy of it.”
sentences.n: liebwerth (modern lieb und wert) is an old flourish of address, roughly “much esteemed.” The fox addresses her throughout as ihr, the deferential plural “you” of the older language where modern German would use Sie; English has only the one word, so the ceremony has to be heard in what is said around it.

sentences.t: Bei dem Fest ließ er sichs schmecken und machte sich ganz lustig, hernach sagte er „liebe Frau Gevatterin, es ist unsere Pflicht, für das Kindlein zu sorgen, ihr müßt gute Nahrung haben, damit es auch zu Kräften kommt.
sentences.l: At the feast he let it taste him well and made himself quite merry; afterwards he said “dear Mistress Godmother, it is our duty to care for the little-child; you must have good nourishment, so that it too comes to strength.
sentences.i: At the feast he ate his fill and made very merry, and afterwards he said: “Dear Mistress Godmother, it is our duty to see to the little one; you must have good nourishment, so that he may come to his strength.
sentences.n: “sich etwas schmecken lassen” — to let something taste good to oneself, i.e. to fall to with a will. sichs is sich es. The duty he invokes is hers; the dinner he is arranging is his.

sentences.t: Ich weiß einen Schafstall, woraus wir leicht ein gutes Stück holen können.“
sentences.l: I know a sheep-fold out of which we can easily fetch a good piece.”
sentences.i: I know a sheepfold where we could easily come by a good piece.”

sentences.t: Der Wölfin gefiel das Liedlein, und sie gieng mit dem Fuchs hinaus nach dem Bauernhof.
sentences.l: The little-song pleased the she-wolf, and she went out with the fox toward the farmyard.
sentences.i: The she-wolf liked that tune well enough, and went out with the fox to the farmyard.
sentences.n: Liedlein, “little song,” for a proposal someone sings in your ear: the tale is already telling you what the offer is worth.

sentences.t: Er zeigte ihr den Stall aus der Ferne und sprach „dort werdet ihr ungesehen hineinkriechen können, ich will mich derweil auf der andern Seite umsehen, ob ich etwa ein Hühnlein erwische.“
sentences.l: He showed her the fold from a distance and said “there you will be able to creep in unseen; I will meanwhile look around on the other side, whether I might catch a little-hen.”
sentences.i: He showed her the fold from a distance and said: “There you will be able to creep in unseen; meanwhile I will look about on the other side, and see whether I can catch myself a hen.”
sentences.n: “werdet ihr … hineinkriechen können” stacks two infinitives at the end after the future werden, and English unpicks them the other way round: will be able to creep in. derweil = meanwhile (modern derweilen).

sentences.t: Er gieng aber nicht hin, sondern ließ sich am Eingang des Waldes nieder, streckte die Beine und ruhte sich.
sentences.l: But he did not go there, but rather let himself down at the entrance of the forest, stretched his legs and rested himself.
sentences.i: But he did not go; he settled himself down at the entrance of the wood, stretched out his legs and took his ease.

sentences.t: Die Wölfin kroch in den Stall, da lag ein Hund und machte Lärm, so daß die Bauern gelaufen kamen, die Frau Gevatterin ertappten und eine scharfe Lauge von ungebrannter Asche über ihr Fell gossen.
sentences.l: The she-wolf crept into the fold; there lay a dog and made a noise, so that the farmers came running, caught Mistress Godmother and poured a sharp lye of unburnt ashes over her fur.
sentences.i: The she-wolf crept into the fold; but a dog was lying there and set up a din, so that the farmers came running, caught Mistress Godmother, and poured a sharp lye of unburnt ashes over her coat.
sentences.n: “ungebrannte Asche” is an old joke, not a recipe: ash that has not yet been burnt is still wood, so a lye of it is a beating with sticks. The tale keeps the polite phrasing and lets the reader do the arithmetic.

sentences.t: Endlich entkam sie doch und schleppte sich hinaus:
sentences.l: At last she did escape after all and dragged herself out:
sentences.n: doch here is concessive — she got out in spite of it all. “sich schleppen” = to drag oneself along.

sentences.t: da lag der Fuchs, that ganz kläglich und sprach „ach, liebe Frau Gevatterin, wie ist mirs schlimm ergangen! die Bauern haben mich überfallen und mir alle Glieder zerschlagen, wenn ihr nicht wollt daß ich auf dem Platz liegen bleiben und verschmachten soll, so müßt ihr mich forttragen.“
sentences.l: there lay the fox, acted quite pitiful and said “ah, dear Mistress Godmother, how badly it has gone with me! the farmers have fallen upon me and beaten all my limbs to pieces; if you do not want that I should stay lying on the spot and perish, then you must carry me away.”
sentences.i: there lay the fox, putting on a wretched face, and said: “Ah, dear Mistress Godmother, how badly I have fared! The farmers set upon me and broke every limb in my body; unless you would have me lie here on the spot and perish, you must carry me away.”
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat (thun/tun). “wie ist mirs ergangen” is impersonal ergehen with the person in the dative — how it went with me; there is no German way to say “I fared” with a plain subject.

sentences.t: Die Wölfin konnte selbst nur langsam fort, doch hatte sie große Sorge für den Fuchs, daß sie ihn auf ihren Rücken nahm, und den ganz gesunden und heilen Gevatter langsam bis zu ihrem Haus trug.
sentences.l: The she-wolf herself could only get on slowly, yet she had such great care for the fox that she took him onto her back, and carried the perfectly sound and whole godfather slowly all the way to her house.
sentences.i: The she-wolf could barely get along herself, and yet she was so concerned for the fox that she took him on her back and carried the perfectly sound and unhurt godfather slowly all the way home.
sentences.n: “konnte selbst nur langsam fort” leaves the verb of motion out after the modal — could only [get] along slowly; German does this freely with fort, hinaus, heim. The daß-clause is consecutive with its so omitted: such great care that …

sentences.t: Da rief er ihr zu „lebt wohl, liebe Frau Gevatterin, und laßt euch den Braten wohl bekommen,“ lachte sie gewaltig aus und sprang fort.
sentences.l: Then he called to her “fare well, dear Mistress Godmother, and let the roast agree with you well,” laughed at her mightily and sprang away.
sentences.i: Then he called after her: “Farewell, dear Mistress Godmother, and much good may the roast do you” — and he laughed her to scorn and bounded off.
sentences.n: “laßt euch etwas wohl bekommen” is the ordinary wish over food, may it do you good; the only roast she has had is her beating. auslachen, to laugh someone to scorn, is separable: “lachte sie… aus.”
